```{r}
#| label: setup

library(jmpost)
```

The `jmpost` package includes data simulation functionality for the included joint models.
The data simulation is based on specifying the longitudinal model and the survival model including link parameters.


## Example


```{r}
#| label: simulate_data

set.seed(129)
sim_data <- SimJointData(
    design = list(
        SimGroup(50, "Arm-A", "Study-X"),
        SimGroup(50, "Arm-B", "Study-X")
    ),
    longitudinal = SimLongitudinalSteinFojo(
        times = c(-2, 1, 30, 90, 150, 210),
        mu_g = log(c(0.005, 0.005)),
        mu_s = log(c(0.06, 0.007)),
        omega_g = 0.3,
        link_dsld = 0.1,
    ),
    survival = SimSurvivalWeibullPH(
        lambda = 1 / 300,
        gamma = 0.97,
        time_max = 2000,
        time_step = 1,
        lambda_cen = 1 / 9000,
        beta_cat = c(
            "A" = 0,
            "B" = -0.1,
            "C" = 0.5
        ),
        beta_cont = 0.3
    )
)
```

This object has `survival` and `longitudinal` components.
```{r}
head(sim_data@survival)
head(sim_data@longitudinal)
```

We can see the trajectory of the tumour size.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(
    sim_data@longitudinal,
    aes(x = time, y = sld, group = subject)
) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~arm)
```

We can also visualise the Kaplan-Meier survival curves.

```{r}
library(survival)
plot(
    survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data = sim_data@survival),
    col = 1:2,
    lwd = 2,
    main = "Overall Survival"
)
legend("topright", col = 1:2, lwd = 2, legend = c("Arm-A", "Arm-B"))
```

## Administrative Cut Off

We may wish to have a fixed maximum study duration and remove any simulated values after that time.
This can be specified as a single fixed value or as a vector if we additionally wish to consider
enrolment time.

```{r}
sim_data_end <- cut_data(sim_data, 700)
plot(
    survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data = sim_data_end@survival),
    col = 1:2,
    lwd = 2,
    main = "Overall Survival (truncated at time=700)"
)
```


## Progression

We might also be interested in time to progression defined as an increase in tumour size over a threshold.
The threshold is based on the minimum observed SLD up to the given time and the relative and absolute growth.
For example we might require the SLD to increase at least 20% and at least 5mm.
We don't include any observations before time 0 in the calculation of the minimum and we don't observe any SLD values 
after progression.
```{r}
sim_data_pd <- add_pfs(
    sim_data_end,
    relative_threshold = 1.2,
    absolute_threshold = 5,
    from_time = 0,
    observed_after = FALSE
)
```

Let's look at the plots again up to progression.

```{r}
ggplot(
    sim_data_pd@longitudinal |> dplyr::filter(observed), # here we only include observed values
    aes(x = time, y = sld, group = subject)
) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~arm)
```

```{r}
plot(
    survfit(Surv(pfs_time, pfs_event) ~ arm, data = sim_data_pd@survival),
    col = 1:2,
    lwd = 2,
    main = "Progression Free Survival"
)
legend("topright", col = 1:2, lwd = 2, legend = c("Arm-A", "Arm-B"))
```

## Model Fitting from Simulated Data

As already descried in the quick start vignette, we can use this data to fit a joint model.

```{r}
os_data <- sim_data_end@survival
long_data <- sim_data_end@longitudinal
joint_data <- DataJoint(
    subject = DataSubject(
        data = os_data,
        subject = "subject",
        arm = "arm",
        study = "study"
    ),
    survival = DataSurvival(
        data = os_data,
        formula = Surv(time, event) ~ cov_cat + cov_cont
    ),
    longitudinal = DataLongitudinal(
        data = long_data,
        formula = sld ~ time,
        threshold = 5
    )
)


sf_model <- JointModel(
    longitudinal = LongitudinalSteinFojo(
        mu_bsld = prior_normal(log(60), 0.2),
        mu_ks = prior_normal(-3, 0.4),
        mu_kg = prior_normal(log(0.005), 0.3),
        centred = TRUE
    ),
    survival = SurvivalWeibullPH(),
    link = linkDSLD()
)
```


```{r}
#| message: false
#| output: false

set.seed(202671)
mcmc_results <- sampleStanModel(
    sf_model,
    data = joint_data,
    iter_sampling = 1000,
    iter_warmup = 500,
    chains = 4,
    parallel_chains = 4,
    step_size = 0.01
)
```


```{r}
#| output: asis

knitr::kable(
    mcmc_results@results$summary(
        c("lm_sf_mu_bsld", "lm_sf_mu_ks", "lm_sf_mu_kg", "lm_sf_omega_bsld", "lm_sf_omega_ks", "lm_sf_omega_ks")
    ),
    digits = 3
)
```

## Posterior correlations

Posterior dependence can help explain uncertainty in the baseline, shrinkage
and growth parameters. We first examine the log random effects for
one patient, then summarise these correlations over all patients. Each
correlation is calculated **across posterior draws for the same patient**.

Here we use `log(psi)`, the patient-specific baseline, shrinkage and growth
parameters on the log scale, including their population locations. These
are available directly from the fitted model without standardisation or
subtracting `mu`. The Stan data map patient IDs to Stan indices and identify
the study and treatment arm used below to select the population means.

```{r}
#| label: sf-posterior-correlation-draws

sf_draws <- mcmc_results |>
    cmdstanr::as.CmdStanMCMC() |>
    posterior::as_draws_matrix() |>
    posterior::subset_draws(
        variables = c(
            "lm_sf_psi_bsld", "lm_sf_psi_ks", "lm_sf_psi_kg",
            "lm_sf_mu_bsld", "lm_sf_mu_ks", "lm_sf_mu_kg"
        )
    )
subject_data <- as_stan_list(joint_data@subject)

# Function to extract log-scale effects for a given patient index i.
log_effect_draws <- function(i) {
    variables <- sprintf("lm_sf_psi_%s[%d]", c("bsld", "ks", "kg"), i)
    log_effects <- log(as.matrix(sf_draws[, variables, drop = FALSE]))
    colnames(log_effects) <- c("Baseline", "Shrinkage", "Growth")
    log_effects
}
```

For illustration, select the first patient in Stan order. The scatterplots
show joint posterior draws, and the matrix contains empirical Pearson
correlations. Chains are pooled after warm-up; check convergence and effective
sample sizes before interpreting these estimates.

```{r}
#| label: sf-patient-posterior-correlations

patient_index <- 1L
patient_id <- names(subject_data$subject_to_index)[subject_data$subject_to_index == patient_index]
patient_log_effects <- log_effect_draws(patient_index)
bayesplot::mcmc_pairs(patient_log_effects)
knitr::kable(cor(patient_log_effects), digits = 3)
```

We can see here that the baseline and growth log-scale effects are strongly negatively correlated. This means that patients with higher baseline values tend to have lower growth effects, and vice versa.

We can repeat the calculation separately for every patient, retaining the three
pairwise correlations per patient. The table summarises their distribution
across patients. Its quantiles describe differences between patients; they
are not posterior credible intervals for a correlation.

```{r}
#| label: sf-all-patient-posterior-correlations

log_effect_correlations <- seq_len(subject_data$n_subjects) |>
    lapply(function(i) cor(log_effect_draws(i)))
pairwise_correlations <- log_effect_correlations |>
    lapply(function(x) {
        c(
            "Baseline / shrinkage" = x[1, 2],
            "Baseline / growth" = x[1, 3],
            "Shrinkage / growth" = x[2, 3]
        )
    }) |>
    dplyr::bind_rows()
rownames(pairwise_correlations) <- names(subject_data$subject_to_index)
correlation_summary <- pairwise_correlations |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(
        cols = dplyr::everything(),
        names_to = "Correlation",
        values_to = "Value"
    ) |>
    dplyr::group_by(.data$Correlation) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
        dplyr::across(
            dplyr::everything(),
            list(
                Mean = ~ mean(.),
                SD = ~ sd(.),
                Min = ~ quantile(., 0),
                Q1 = ~ quantile(., 0.25),
                Median = ~ quantile(., 0.5),
                Q3 = ~ quantile(., 0.75),
                Max = ~ quantile(., 1)
            )
        )
    )
knitr::kable(correlation_summary, digits = 3)
```

We can also inspect posterior correlations between the population location
parameters `mu`, on their modelled log scale. Here we select the study and
arm of the illustrated patient; repeat for other arms or studies as needed.
These are correlations between uncertain population parameters, rather than
correlations between patient effects.

```{r}
#| label: sf-population-posterior-correlations

mu_names <- c("lm_sf_mu_bsld[1]", "lm_sf_mu_ks[1]", "lm_sf_mu_kg[1]")
mu_draws <- as.matrix(sf_draws[, mu_names, drop = FALSE])
colnames(mu_draws) <- c("Baseline", "Shrinkage", "Growth")
bayesplot::mcmc_pairs(mu_draws)
knitr::kable(cor(mu_draws), digits = 3)
```

The model specifies independent priors for the patient effects. Posterior
correlations can nevertheless arise because the likelihood couples baseline,
shrinkage and growth. Neither the within-patient correlations nor their
summary across patients estimates a population random-effects correlation
parameter.

## Simulating from a Fitted Model

The package also have the functionality to generate new data based on the fitted model.
We use the [simulate.JointModelSamples] function.

```{r}
?simulate.JointModelSamples
set.seed(198802)
new_model_data <- simulate(
    mcmc_results,
    times = c(-2, 1, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180),
    jitter_var = c(0, 2)
)
```

For this simulation we set 

- the times we wish to have longitudinal observations
- variance for jitter around those observation times
- time_max and time_step for numerical integration
- lambda parameter for exponential censoring times
- scaled_variance which should be set to the same as the fitted model. This is described more in 
  the statistical specifications vignette.

Now we can inspect the new simulated data.

```{r}
head(new_model_data@longitudinal)
head(new_model_data@survival)
```


```{r}
ggplot(
    dplyr::bind_rows(
        "model sim" = new_model_data@longitudinal,
        "original data" = sim_data@longitudinal,
        .id = "sim"
    ),
    aes(x = time, y = sld, group = subject)
) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.1) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~ arm + sim) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 400)) +
    ggtitle("Original Data versus Model Simulated Data")
```

```{r}
plot(
    survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data = new_model_data@survival),
    col = 1:2,
    lwd = 2,
    main = "Overall Survival (simulated from model)"
)
lines(
    survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ arm, data = sim_data@survival),
    col = 1:2,
    lwd = 2,
    lty = 2
)
legend("topright",
    col = c(1, 2, 1, 2), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
    legend = c("Arm-A from model", "Arm-B from model", "Arm-A original", "Arm-B original")
)
```
